author: deadstrobe5
body:
#### References to other Issues or PRs

Speeds up the cases in #10697 and #22240 (does not close them).

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed

`Basic._subs` calls `_aresame(self, old)` on every node, and the fallback calls `_aresame` on every argument. Each call walked both subtrees in postorder, so a substitution cost roughly size times depth and was paid again for each pair in the mapping.

When `approx` is None, `is_same` now returns True for the same object, returns False when the root classes differ (the old walk always ended with that same class check at the root), and compares two arg-less Basic leaves with `==` directly. The loop also tests `a is None or b is None` instead of `None in t`, which called `Basic.__eq__(None)` twice per node. The `approx` path is unchanged.

Same-process A/B on CPython 3.14, median of 5 alternating runs, cache cleared before each run:

| case | before | after | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8x8 Matrix.subs with a 200-symbol dict | 4872 ms | 1062 ms | 4.6x |
| `((x+1)**2 + 1).subs(d)`, 3000-key dict (#10697) | 494 ms | 97 ms | 5.1x |
| expanded `(x+y+z+w+1)**10`, `subs(x, t+1)` | 117 ms | 59 ms | 2.0x |
| small expr subs x2000 | 652 ms | 454 ms | 1.4x |
| `x.subs(x, k)` x5000 | 72 ms | 25 ms | 2.9x |

#### Other comments

A differential fuzz of the old and new `is_same` (and `subs`, `subs(simultaneous=True)`) over about 14,500 random expression pairs, including numbers, Floats, Tuples, non-commutative symbols, Python ints and the `equal_valued` approx, found no difference. The new test covers equal-but-distinct `UndefinedFunction` classes, which must still compare the same.

#### AI Generation Disclosure

Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5) wrote all of the code and tests in this PR and ran the benchmarks and the old-vs-new comparisons quoted above.

#### Release Notes

<!-- BEGIN RELEASE NOTES -->
* core
  * `subs` is faster, up to 5x for substitutions with large dicts, because `Basic.is_same` no longer walks identical or differently typed subtrees.
<!-- END RELEASE NOTES -->

linked.author: asmeurer
linked.body:
If you have a large mapping, subs iterates over each term in the mapping, even if `simultaneous=True`. Contrast this with `xreplace`, which does the substitution all at once.

```
In [18]: a = (x + 1)**2 + 1

In [19]: mapping = {Symbol('x%d' % i): i for i in range(10000)}

In [20]: %timeit a.subs(mapping)
1 loop, best of 3: 4.93 s per loop

In [21]: %timeit a.subs(mapping, simultaneous=True)
1 loop, best of 3: 8.04 s per loop

In [22]: %timeit a.xreplace(mapping)
100000 loops, best of 3: 11.5 µs per loop
```

`subs` should only traverse an expression once when `simultaneous=True` (side note: I agree with the `XXX` comment in the code, simultaneous=True should be the default for dictionaries, maybe even the default always, but that's another issue). Even when simultaneous=False, it may be faster to recursively apply subs recursively to the mapping (in reverse), remove duplicates, and then apply the mapping all at once to the expression. We'd have to test it, but I suspect it would be faster, since in the common case the expression will be large and the terms in the mapping will be small.
linked.title: subs is too slow for large mappings

linked.author: nguyenthanhvuh
linked.body: Hi, it seems that the `.subs` function is quite slow. When I have a long expression `e` (can contain nonlinear terms like `x**2, y*x*z`), calling `e.subs(some_dict)` takes some noticeable time (two sec's or so). In fact `subs` is often slower than solving  large equations. Is there something obvious that I miss ?  My main goal is to just substitute variables in the expression with concrete values,   e.g.,  `x*y.subs({x:3}) = 3*y`
linked.title: subs is slow

With that, then the following will pass (and should be added to tests):
```python
f1 = float('nan')
f2 = float('nan')
b1 = Basic(f1)
b2 = Basic(f1)

assert f1 is not f2
assert b1 is not b2

assert _aresame(f1, f1)
assert not _aresame(f1, f2)
assert _aresame(b1, b1)
assert _aresame(b1, b2)
assert not _aresame(b1, Basic(f2))

assert not _aresame(f1, S.NaN)
assert not _aresame(b1, Basic(S.NaN))
```
